subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: An 'extended family' is best defined as:
options: A nuclear family plus other relatives such as grandparents, aunts or uncles
Any group of friends sharing a house
A married couple and their dependent children only
questions.explain: The extended family includes relatives beyond the nuclear unit, such as grandparents or aunts and uncles.

questions.q: Murdock argued the nuclear family performs four essential functions. Which is one of them?
questions.explain: Murdock identified four functions: sexual, reproductive, economic and educational (socialisation).

questions.q: Parsons argued the modern nuclear family has two 'irreducible' functions. Which pair did he identify?
options: Primary socialisation of children and stabilisation of adult personalities
questions.explain: Parsons claimed the family's two essential functions are the primary socialisation of children and the stabilisation of adult personalities.

questions.q: Which sociologist studied 250 societies and argued the nuclear family is universal?
questions.explain: George Murdock examined 250 societies and claimed the nuclear family performed four essential functions everywhere.

questions.q: Marxist Friedrich Engels argued that the monogamous nuclear family developed mainly to:
options: Ensure the inheritance of private property through legitimate heirs
questions.explain: Engels argued monogamy arose so men could pass private property to legitimate heirs.

questions.q: Increased cohabitation and rising divorce have contributed to greater:
options: The end of the nuclear family entirely
questions.explain: Such changes have produced greater family diversity, with many household types now common.

questions.q: A 'beanpole family' is one that is:
options: Made up only of unrelated adults
Wide, with many cousins in each generation
Tall and thin, with several living generations but few children per generation
questions.explain: A beanpole family has multiple living generations but few members within each generation, reflecting smaller family sizes.

questions.q: A 'single-person household' is one where:
options: A couple live with one child
questions.explain: A single-person household consists of just one person living alone, a growing category in the UK.

questions.q: Parsons argued that, as society industrialised, the dominant family type shifted from the extended family towards the:
questions.explain: Parsons argued industrial society favoured the geographically mobile, isolated nuclear family.

questions.q: Which feminist sociologist's research found that few couples genuinely shared housework equally, challenging the 'symmetrical family'?
questions.explain: Ann Oakley criticised Young and Willmott, finding the domestic division of labour remained largely unequal.

questions.q: One reason given for the rise in lone-parent families is:
options: A fall in the divorce rate
Rising divorce and more births outside marriage
questions.explain: Higher divorce rates and more births outside marriage have contributed to the growth of lone-parent families.

questions.q: 'Cohabitation' refers to:
options: A couple who are legally married
A couple living together in a relationship without being married
questions.explain: Cohabitation means an unmarried couple living together as partners.

questions.q: Which of these is a likely reason for the rise in divorce rates since the 1960s?
options: Changes in the law making divorce easier and cheaper
questions.explain: Legal changes such as the 1969 Divorce Reform Act made divorce more accessible, contributing to rising rates.

questions.q: The Marxist view of the family argues that the family mainly functions to:
options: Reproduce and maintain capitalism by socialising children to accept inequality
Promote gender equality in the home
questions.explain: Marxists argue the family serves capitalism by reproducing labour power and teaching acceptance of hierarchy.

questions.q: The 'family life course' approach emphasises that:
options: Family life is varied and changes over time and between individuals
All families are identical at every stage
questions.explain: The life-course approach stresses the diversity of family arrangements and how they change over a person's life.

questions.q: The trend in UK marriage rates over recent decades has generally been:
options: A steady decline, with people marrying later or not at all
questions.explain: Marriage rates have fallen and the average age of marriage has risen, alongside more cohabitation.

questions.q: Feminists who study the family often highlight the 'triple shift', meaning women do:
options: Paid work, housework and emotional work
questions.explain: The triple shift refers to women combining paid employment, domestic labour and emotional work for the family.

questions.q: 'Segregated conjugal roles' describe a relationship in which:
options: Partners have clearly separate roles and spend leisure time apart
Partners share tasks and leisure equally
questions.explain: Segregated conjugal roles involve a clear division between male and female tasks, contrasting with joint roles.

questions.q: Young and Willmott's concept of the 'symmetrical family' describes a family in which:
options: Roles of husband and wife have become more similar and shared
The wife does all the domestic work
Extended kin live in the same house
questions.explain: Young and Willmott argued conjugal roles were becoming more joint and similar, calling this the symmetrical family.

questions.q: The 'dark side of the family' refers to:
options: Families who decorate their homes darkly
Families who only meet at night
Negative experiences such as domestic violence, abuse and neglect within families
questions.explain: The 'dark side' highlights that families can also be sites of conflict, abuse, neglect and violence.

questions.q: A 'same-sex family' became more visible in the UK partly because of which legal change?
options: The legalisation of same-sex marriage in 2014
questions.explain: Same-sex marriage was legalised in England and Wales in 2014, increasing recognition of same-sex families.

questions.q: What is a 'reconstituted' family?
options: A family living with grandparents and other relatives
A family headed by one parent only
A married couple with no children
A step-family formed when partners with existing children form a new household
questions.explain: A reconstituted (step) family forms when at least one partner brings children from a previous relationship.
